content: Stretch marks, also known as striae or striae atrophicae in dermatological terminology, are a type of scarring on the skin that typically appears with a silvery-white hue. These marks result from tearing of the dermis, the middle layer of the skin, and while they may fade over time, they do not completely disappear. The skin, despite its elasticity, can develop permanent stretch marks when subjected to rapid stretching, such as during pregnancy, significant weight gain, or rapid muscle growth often associated with steroid use. Stretch marks are also referred to as striae distensae, and in medical contexts, they may be described using terms like striae gravidarum (when caused by pregnancy), lineae atrophicae, or linea albicante. Initially, stretch marks present as reddish or purplish lines, which gradually fade to a lighter color. The affected areas often feel soft and appear empty to the touch. Human skin consists of three layers: the epidermis (outer layer), the dermis (middle layer), and the subcutaneous stratum (innermost layer). Stretch marks form in the dermis, which is the resilient layer responsible for maintaining the skin's shape. As long as the dermis remains supported, stretch marks are unlikely to form. However, the direction and location of the marks are influenced by the stretching forces applied to the skin. Stretching alone is not the sole cause; hormonal and structural factors also play a role. Stretch marks can appear anywhere on the body but are most commonly found in areas where fat is stored, such as the abdomen (especially near the belly button), breasts, upper arms, underarms, thighs (both inner and outer), hips, and buttocks. While they do not pose any health risks or impair the body's ability to function or repair itself, they are often a cosmetic concern. The development of stretch marks is influenced by glucocorticoid hormones, which inhibit fibroblasts from producing collagen and elastin fibers—key components that maintain skin tautness during rapid growth. This lack of supportive material leads to tearing in the dermis and epidermis. If the damage penetrates both layers, treatments like laser therapy cannot completely remove the stretch marks. During pregnancy, between 75% and 90% of women develop stretch marks to some degree, typically appearing in the sixth or seventh month due to sustained hormonal changes. Research on prevention is limited. One randomized controlled study found that daily application of a cream containing Centella asiatica extract, vitamin E, and collagen-elastin hydrolysates (e.g., Trofolastin) was associated with fewer stretch marks during pregnancy. Another study, though lacking a placebo control, suggested that a cream containing vitamin E, panthenol, hyaluronic acid, elastin, and menthol (e.g., Verum) also reduced the incidence of stretch marks compared to no treatment. However, there is no evidence to support the effectiveness of cocoa butter in preventing or improving stretch marks. Various treatments aim to improve the appearance of existing stretch marks, including laser treatments, dermabrasion, and prescription retinoids. These treatments, when used daily for a month, have shown significant improvements in the length, depth, and surface irregularities of stretch marks. Some manufacturers claim better results on recent stretch marks, but supporting studies are limited. Pulsed dye lasers have been shown to increase pigmentation in darker-skinned individuals with repeated treatments. Surgical options, such as a tummy tuck, can remove lower abdominal stretch marks by excising the skin below the navel. A newer approach, fractional laser resurfacing, offers a novel treatment for stretch marks. This technique uses scattered pulses of light to target only a fraction of the scar tissue during each session, creating microscopic wounds. This no downtime procedure stimulates the body to produce new collagen and epithelial tissue in response to each treatment. Clinical trials in 2007 demonstrated that 5-6 sessions of fractional laser therapy improved stretch marks by up to 75%. A Brazilian study also showed that fractional photothermolysis (e.g., Fraxel) improved the texture and appearance of mature, white stretch marks in skin types I-IV.
